current_text.html: Courts may sometimes entirely neglect to perform their duty, by which neglect heretical opinions or corrupt practices may be allowed to gain ground; or offenders of a very gross character may be suffered to escape; or some circumstances in their proceedings of very great irregularity may not be distinctly recorded by them. In any of these cases their records will by no means exhibit to the higher court a full view of their proceedings. If, therefore, the next higher court be well advised that any such neglect or irregularity has occurred on the part of the lower court, it is incumbent on it to take cognizance of the same, and to examine, deliberate and judge in the whole matter as completely as if it had been recorded, and thus brought up by review of its records.

metadata.synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

metadata.synopsis: Presbytery investigated a Session's handling of sexual-misconduct allegations and found it guilty of delinquencies without a trial. The SJC upheld Presbytery's authority to receive credible reports and investigate, but annulled the findings of guilt, censures, and corrective mandates because BCO 40-6 required formal process or an admission before censure. It returned the matter for records review, informal resolution, or formal process and declined interim mandates that would assume the disputed allegations were true.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained a complaint against Philadelphia Presbytery for failing to judge and record TE Larry Smith’s stated difference over the continuation of prophecy and tongues beyond the apostolic era. The record showed Presbytery approved Smith’s transfer exam and defeated a motion to find his view out of accord, but it did not categorize that view in Smith’s own words. The SJC remanded for a written statement and Presbytery’s categorical judgment, without undoing Smith’s transfer or deciding whether his view was erroneous.

relationships.title: Anna Lewis v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley

occurrences.excerpt: …As such, this matter is squarely within the circumstances contemplated by BCO 40-4... (M36GA, p. 84)

metadata.synopsis: After her session erased her from the roll, Anna Lewis filed a BCO 40-5 report directly with the SJC, alleging the Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley failed to redress the session's alleged failure to give BCO 38-4 notice. The SJC held the filing out of order: under RAO 16-10.c and OMSJC Chapter 15, BCO Chapter 40 matters come to it only by General Assembly referral. It did not decide the merits, but noted that without proper notice Lewis remains a member unless she joined another church. Dissents disputed that limitation and cited past direct reviews.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
metadata.synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

metadata.synopsis: Jackson challenged Northwest Georgia Presbytery’s failure to act on his BCO 40-5 letter alleging delinquency by Midway’s Session. The SJC found his complaint administratively out of order and dismissed it because he was not a commissioner at Presbytery’s January 2013 meeting; originating a BCO 40-5 report did not confer standing. Separately, the SJC accepted jurisdiction over Presbytery’s failure to respond and remitted the matter for constitutional disposition, without deciding whether the Session committed the alleged delinquencies.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

metadata.synopsis: A Session appealed Presbytery’s judgment finding it guilty and suspending it for refusing instructions to institute process against a member. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed the judgment in whole, and dismissed the charges. Once Presbytery denied the member’s complaint, that matter should have ended; moreover, Presbytery did not follow BCO 40-4’s required first step before invoking BCO 40-5 review and control. The delay, prejudice, and missing-witness specifications were moot. The decision did not fault Presbytery’s underlying concern.

relationships.title: the Session of Hope Community Church v. Central Carolina Presbytery

topics: session authority over time and place of worship
metadata.synopsis: Hope Community Church’s Session challenged Presbytery’s requirement that a multi-site congregation eventually particularize its second worship site. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled the requirement, and struck it from the Presbytery Manual because BCO 12-5e specifically entrusts the time and place of worship to the Session, which Presbytery’s general church-enlargement authority could not supersede. The narrow ruling did not resolve broader concerns about multi-site churches or eliminate Presbytery’s review of a second site’s location under BCO 13-9(g).

relationships.title: William G. Mitchell v. The Presbytery of the Ascension

metadata.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed judgments concerning an alleged broken promise to take a sabbatical and deficient performance as Session clerk. Because the pivotal email was absent from the record, the SJC vacated the sabbatical-related judgment and remanded for Presbytery only to consider whether a new trial was warranted. It reversed and dismissed the clerk-duty specification because the four-month delay in submitting minutes was attributable to the Session and did not justify a trial. Only the first specification remained potentially triable.

relationships.title: PCA v. Korean Capital Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The 40th General Assembly cited Korean Capital Presbytery for failing to respond to substantive exceptions in its October 6, 2008 minutes. The SJC noted that the Presbytery had submitted responses approved by the Presbytery under BCO 10-4 and found those responses acceptable. The record does not state a dismissal, acquittal, or other formal merits disposition; the matter is an administrative BCO 40-5 citation resolved by acceptance of the Presbytery's responses.

relationships.title: Presbyterian Church in America v. Warrior Presbytery

topics: Committee on Review of Presbytery Records
metadata.synopsis: The 39th General Assembly cited Warrior Presbytery under BCO 40 provisions for failing to answer exceptions of substance in several meeting minutes. The SJC recorded that the Presbytery had since submitted responses approved by the Presbytery and found them acceptable. The adopted ruling provides no further rationale or separate relief.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
metadata.synopsis: A complaint challenged Siouxlands Presbytery's investigation of allegations that TE Joshua Moon held heterodox Federal Vision views and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC held that Presbytery had investigated diligently under BCO 31-2 and, deferring under BCO 39-3 to its credibility judgment, found no clear error. It declined to decide whether the overture should have been treated as charges because that issue was not raised below, while leaving future charges possible. A concurrence favored charges; the dissent would have found error and remanded.

metadata.synopsis: Pacific Northwest Presbytery adopted a report finding TE Peter Leithart's views not out of accord with the fundamentals of the system of doctrine. The SJC sustained a complaint, holding PNW erred because, without formal judicial process, it lacked authority to declare either that the views were out of accord or that they were not. The record still suggested a strong presumption of guilt. The SJC refused complainants' affirmative declaration and remanded with directions for pastoral counsel under BCO 31-7 and possible BCO 31-2 compliance.

metadata.synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

metadata.synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. metadata.synopsis: In this BCO 40-5 proceeding over Louisiana Presbytery’s investigation of TE Stephen Wilkins, the SJC dismissed Specification 1 because it could not find that the cited procedures were constitutionally required or that guilt was proved. The dismissal did not erase concerns about undocumented doctrinal findings; those failures were covered by Specification 2. On Presbytery’s guilty plea to that specification, the SJC imposed a public admonition for failing to find a strong presumption of doctrinal guilt and pursue trial. Wilkins’s and his church’s withdrawal made practical amends unavailable.

relationships.title: Clark v. Southwest Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: TE John P. Clark, Jr. appealed his conviction for contumacy and suspension/deposition by Southwest Presbytery's Judicial Commission. The SJC found the appeal in order (17-4) and remanded the case for retrial (21-0) on grounds that the Judicial Commission committed significant procedural errors, including abandoning original charges and convicting Clark of contumacy on new charges without giving him opportunity to respond.

relationships.title: Grace RPC Session v. Heartland Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: TE Steve Newton appealed his conviction for contumacy and indefinite suspension from office by Heartland Presbytery's judicial commission for persistent failure to submit statistical reports and refusal to cooperate with Presbytery committees. The SJC affirmed Heartland Presbytery's judgment in all respects, with a concurring opinion finding three of four specifications invalid but deferring to the lower court's factfinding on the remaining specification.

relationships.title: Chappell v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery

topics: suspension of session without due process
metadata.synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

relationships.title: Marshall v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery

topics: suspension of session without due process
metadata.synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'
